newsitem.title: IRAQ: FOCUS-Iraq expects oil exports again by mid-August.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Iraq expects oil exports again by mid-August.

text.p: Iraq expects to resume oil exports under its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations in mid-August, Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed said on Wednesday.
"In our minds we are expecting to resume oil exports at the middle of August," Rasheed told reporters in Baghdad.

Iraq had delayed exports under the UN scheme to modify plans for aid distribution. The programme was set up to alleviate the impact on civilians of sanctions imposed on Iraq after its troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Rasheed said Iraq would do its best to meet a permitted $2 billion target for oil sales by the deadline for the second phase of the U.N. agreement.
"We are going to export the amount which is $2 billion worth of oil before December 6," he said, without elaborating.
Under the terms of the deal Iraq is allowed to export $2.14 billion of oil, including $140 million for Turkish pipeline feeds, over 180 days in two equal instalments starting from June 8.
Exports were delayed while a new aid distribution plan was put in place, meaning Baghdad must sell around $1 billion of oil by September 5 or forego some of its allowance.
Rasheed indicated Iraq's export capacity currently was 1.8 million bpd. He said Iraqi production capacity was 2.5 million bpd including 700,000 bpd for domestic consumption.

Exports under the first six-month phase of the agreement which started last December averaged nearly 700,000 bpd in shipments from Turkey's Ceyhan terminal on the Mediterranean and Iraq's Gulf port Mina al-Bakr.
The minister said contracts as soon as UN approval for new oil sales formula was received.
"There are several oil companies currently in Baghdad seeking to buy Iraqi crude and we have many offers (from oil firms)," he added.
Rasheed said his country, restricted to Mina al-Bakr for exports from its own territory, was ready to resume oil sales via the Iraqi-Syrian pipeline, closed since early 1980s.
"We are prepared to resume (oil) pumping via Syria whenever the Syrian government takes a decision to resume pumping," he said.
He said it was up to the Syrian government to open the line again.
"The decision to stop oil pumping across Syrian, was Syrian," he said.
In the past two months there have been hints of a rapprochement between Iraq and Syria, ruled by rival factions of the Baath party.
On Jordan, the oil minister said Iraq supported building an Iraqi-Jordanian pipeline. He gave no further details.
Jordan, which is exempt from United Nations sanctions that bar Iraq from freely exporting its oil following its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, imports about 80,000 bpd from Iraq.
